one_liner: Rust framework for HTTP/1, HTTP/2, WebSocket and TLS services; in HttpArena it edges Drogon on keep-alive requests but loses on connection churn.
what_it_does: ntex is a toolkit of crates (ntex-io, ntex-server, ntex-rt, ntex-http, ntex-router, ntex-tls, ntex-util, ntex-bytes) for building network services, with an actix-web-like web layer on top: App, resource routes, extractors (Path, Query, Json, Bytes, State), middleware (Logger, Compress, DefaultHeaders), HTTP/2 via ntex-h2, WebSockets, an HTTP client and rustls or OpenSSL TLS. HttpServer takes an App factory and runs one copy per worker thread. MQTT, AMQP and gRPC live in sibling repos on the same I/O stack. It is an application framework, not a drop-in for Drogon's C++ API or for nginx.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker thread runs its own single-threaded runtime (thread-per-core, no work-stealing), so services and state use Rc and Cell instead of Arc and locks. Ntex 2.x can run on tokio, compio or its own neon runtime, and ntex 4 defaults to a native io_uring reactor on Linux. Reads and writes go through ntex-io filter buffers drawn from ntex-bytes memory pools (PoolId). HTTP/1 heads are parsed with httparse into a stack array of uninitialised header slots, the Date header is cached by a per-thread DateService, and keep-alive and read-rate timeouts run on a hierarchical timer wheel with 16 ms ticks (ntex-util time/wheel.rs, modelled on the Linux kernel timer wheel), which keeps timers cheap but coarse.
when_to_use: Rust HTTP/1.1 APIs that want framework features (routing, extractors, middleware, TLS) with keep-alive throughput in Drogon's class: HttpArena baseline-4096 gives 2,168,712 req/s vs Drogon 2,022,710 and Cutelyst 2,153,860 on a Threadripper PRO 3995WX (server on 32 cores / 64 threads).
JSON over TLS with many keep-alive clients: json-tls-4096 reached 1,254,763 req/s at 159 MiB RSS, level with h2o (1,229,462) and close to nginx (1,313,755).
Services that also speak MQTT, AMQP or gRPC and want one runtime and buffer model across protocols (ntex-mqtt, ntex-amqp, ntex-grpc).
Deployments that want to choose the I/O backend per build: tokio, compio, or the native polling or io_uring reactor through Cargo features.
Memory-lean servers: HttpArena RSS was 40-148 MiB on most profiles, against Drogon's 1.3 GiB on limited-conn-4096.
when_not_to_use: Connection churn (short-lived connections): limited-conn-4096 (10 requests per connection) gives 1,449,176 req/s, slower than Drogon 1,694,883 and Cutelyst 1,736,401.

Top plain HTTP/1.1 throughput: nginx 3,284,513, h2o 3,641,609, libreactorng 4,377,377 and actix-web 2,775,120 all beat it on baseline-4096. At a pinned 1M req/s it spent 35.03 us of CPU per request vs Drogon 32.13 us, and on 8 logical CPUs it held 337,940 of the 500,000 req/s offered vs Drogon 374,962.
Sub-16 ms sleeps or timeouts: ntex::time::sleep rounds up to the 16 ms wheel tick (UNITS = 4 in ntex-util 2.16 and still on main). The HttpArena 10 ms delay averaged 30.63 ms.

Teams that need a stable API: 3.0 shipped 2026-02-02 and 4.0 on 2026-10-08. 4.x reversed middleware registration order on purpose (issue #1106, documented only in the migration guide) and changed HttpServer::bind to take a SharedCfg.

Production use of the new default io_uring reactor without testing: issue #932 (ntex 3.10.0 with ntex-bytes 1.7.6) served stale bytes at the start of static-file bodies until ntex-net 1.13.1, #911 reported flaky first requests on io-uring, and #1113 (open) says Compress gzips the empty body of a 304.

integration.form: crate (ntex 4.2.0 on crates.io; workspace crates ntex-io, ntex-server, ntex-rt, ntex-net, ntex-http, ntex-router, ntex-tls, ntex-util, ntex-bytes, ntex-service)
integration.dependencies: httparse, http types, serde, serde_json, serde_urlencoded, log, bitflags, slab, futures-timer, nanorand and the ntex-* workspace crates; optional tokio, compio, polling or io-uring, rustls or openssl, flate2 (zlib-rs backend since 4.2.0) and zstd for compress, cookie
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.97 for ntex 4.x (README MSRV badge and crates.io rust_version); the ntex 2.18.0 that HttpArena measured needs Rust 1.82
integration.platforms: Linux (io_uring with polling fallback, or tokio/compio), other Unix (polling), Windows (IOCP); CI runs on Linux, macOS and Windows
integration.thread_safety: One single-threaded runtime per worker. The App factory runs once per worker and services are !Send (Rc-based), so shared state is passed through State and cloned or Arc-wrapped per worker. Worker count defaults to core_affinity::get_core_ids() (the CPU affinity set), else available_parallelism.

gotchas: Version gap: the HttpArena entry pins ntex = "2" with the tokio feature, which resolves to 2.18.0 (2026-02-01). Current ntex is 4.2.0 (2026-10-10), two breaking majors later, with a native io_uring runtime by default on Linux, so none of the measured rows describe ntex 4.

The async-32000 lead (963,884 vs Drogon 143,001 req/s, 6.7x) measures the two entries' timer choices, not HTTP stack speed. ntex's 16 ms timer tick turns the 10 ms delay into a 30.63 ms average, which caps it near 32,000 / 33 ms. Drogon's handler schedules every delay with app().getLoop(), which Drogon documents as the framework's main event loop rather than an I/O loop, so all 32,000 timers run on one thread (812% CPU, 221 ms average latency).

The json-comp lead (589,934 vs 127,466 req/s, 4.6x) compares unequal work. ntex gzips in the handler at flate2 level 1 (flate2 1.x default backend). Drogon's stock enableGzip path calls deflateInit2 with Z_DEFAULT_COMPRESSION (level 6), and its handler deep-copies jsoncpp Values per item. Bandwidth divided by req/s gives about 1,718 bytes per ntex response vs 1,393 for Drogon (derived from page data). The profile retires each connection after 25 requests (-r 25), so the 116,073 reconnects are by design.

Harness asymmetry against ntex: the entry wraps the App in middleware::Logger::default().exclude("/"). No route is "/", so every request calls SystemTime::now, clones the log format and renders the request line, remote address, Referer and User-Agent into heap Strings, then boxes the body in a StreamLog. No logger is installed, so the output is discarded, while Drogon runs at log level kError. The baseline, limited-conn and latency rows probably understate a Logger-free ntex, by an amount not measured.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick actix-web over ntex for the larger ecosystem and its higher baseline-4096 score (2,775,120 vs 2,168,712 req/s). Pick ntex when you want one stack for HTTP, MQTT, AMQP and gRPC, or a build-time choice of tokio, compio or native io_uring. The raw tokio, tokio-uring, zix and zeemo HttpArena entries (3.5-4.4M req/s) are minimal benchmark servers, not frameworks.
verified_claims_summary: HttpArena ran ntex 2.18 on tokio (rustc 1.94, opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, no LTO, no target-cpu=native) against Drogon (CMake Release from drogonframework/drogon:latest, jemalloc preloaded, no -march=native) on a Threadripper PRO 3995WX, with the server on 32 cores / 64 threads and the gcannon load generator on the other half, best of three 5 s runs. ntex leads Drogon by 1.07x on baseline-4096 and trails it 0.86x on limited-conn-4096; the large json-comp, json-tls and async leads come from Drogon-entry choices (level-6 gzip, jsoncpp copies, a single timer loop). Per the verified record, TechEmpower Round 22 plaintext had ntex [raw] at 7,000,539 vs cinatra 6,998,076 and lithium 6,993,976, a 0.1% tie with unknown build flags.
status_note: Very active: 4.2.0 released 2026-10-10 after 4.0.0 on 2026-10-08, 5,458 commits, 2.5k stars, about 1.1M crates.io downloads, 3 open issues, dual MIT or Apache-2.0. Copyable as a dependency, but expect API breaks between majors.
